---
title: "quarto-index dangling cross-reference probe"
from: markdown-smart
filters:
  - index
---

# A cross-reference target that names no index entry

"Cats, see Felines" sends a reader to an entry the index does not have. The
target is not dropped — what the author wrote is theirs (IP2) — but it is
reported, in every format, because whether a target names a term the document
indexes is a fact about the document rather than about a back-end.

The criterion shape: this document indexes `Cats`, and a mark points at
`Felines`, which nothing here indexes. [cats]{.index entry="Cats"} is the
entry that exists; [lions]{.index entry="Lions" see="Felines"} points at the
one that does not.

# Every shape the report has to fire on

Varied in form as well as in position, so that no single shape stands in for
the family.

A dangling `see-also=` beside a resolving `see=`, on one mark: the resolving
half must stay silent while the other is reported, and the both-attributes
report fires as it always does. [pumas]{.index entry="Pumas" see="Cats"
see-also="Ocelots"}.

The inversion — a dangling `see=` beside a resolving `see-also=` — so that
neither attribute is the one the report happens to read:
[jaguars]{.index entry="Jaguars" see="Servals" see-also="Cats"}.

A multi-level target, none of whose levels this document indexes:
[caracals]{.index entry="Caracals" see="Wild!Cats!Small"}.

A partial-path target, where the FIRST level is indexed and the second is
not. This is the shape a resolution rule that stops at the first level would
pass and a reader would still be sent nowhere:
[margays]{.index entry="Margays" see="Cats!Kittens"}.

One dangling target written on two separate marks. The report is per mark per
target, not per distinct target: each mark is its own place in the source for
the author to go and fix. [ocelots]{.index entry="Ocelots Marked"
see="Lynxes"} and [bobcats]{.index entry="Bobcats" see="Lynxes"}.
